title: Noble character
hookLine: a prayer for the best character that keeps talking about enemies
tomorrow: who is anyone better than? one last speech answered it.

lines: A PRAYER WITH AN ODD SHAPE.
cards: Ask for one trait and the list writes itself: confident, focused, calm under pressure. Interview answers, profiles and new-year lists all lean the same way, toward traits that look good on you.
An old prayer called noble character has a stranger shape. It opens with the big things: the best faith, the best certainty, the best intentions.
Then it spends line after line on people who cheat you, cut you off, and talk behind your back. Why would a prayer for your own character keep talking about your enemies?

teach.b: Because that's where character shows. The prayer is in the Sahifa of Imam Zayn al-Abidin, and its title is Makarim al-Akhlaq: the noble traits, the best of character.
In Malik's Muwatta, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported to have said he was sent to perfect good character. So the imam asks for it.
First the foundations: faith at its fullest, certainty at its best, intentions at their finest. Then he gets specific.
He asks God to turn the hatred of those who hate him into love, and the envy of the envious into affection. And then the hardest lines.

Help me, he asks, to answer the one who cheats me with good counsel, the one who cuts me off with reaching out, the one who keeps from me with giving, and the one who speaks ill of me with speaking well.
Now the puzzle solves itself. Being gracious to gracious people takes no character at all. Character is the reply.
The prayer doesn't ask to feel nothing when wronged.

teach.h: A BETTER REPLY THAN THE WRONG.
teach.b: It asks for a better answer than the wrong deserved.
The noblest character, here, is measured in replies.

how: Muslims who use the Sahifa read Makarim al-Akhlaq aloud or alone, in Arabic or in translation; teachers often pair it with the report that the Prophet was sent to perfect good character.

o: the best traits, shown most in how you answer a wrong
a family's honor and good name in the community
manners and etiquette at the table and in public

games.q: the wrong, and the reply the prayer asks for — tap the pairs.

s: the prayer asks to stop feeling hurt when wronged
it asks for a better reply, not for no feeling.
it asks to answer the one who cuts you off by reaching out
cutting off is answered with joining, in the prayer's own pattern.
the Muwatta reports the Prophet was sent to perfect good character
the prayer asks for the very thing he was sent to perfect.

games.q: a coworker took credit for your idea in a meeting, and now asks you to look over their slides. which reply fits the prayer?
o: help them well, and talk to them about the credit, calmly and honestly.
help them carelessly; noble character doesn't mean being a doormat.
help them well and say nothing; noble means never bringing it up.
games.why: the prayer asks to answer one who cheats you with good counsel: real help, and honest advice. it's not revenge, and it's not silence either.

practice: Pick one trait from the prayer: good counsel for someone who cheated you, reaching out to someone who cut you off, kind words about someone who talks about you.
Write it by hand on a scrap of paper, and under it, one name: the person it would be hardest to show it to. Keep the paper in front of you for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Noble character: makarim al-akhlaq, the noble traits; in the Sahifa, a prayer that measures them by how you answer a wrong.

orig.note: Arabic: makarim al-akhlaq, the noble traits of character, the prayer's title in the Sahifa.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the noblest character answers a wrong with something better than it deserved. Day 1640, done.

sources.ref: Al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya 20 (Makarim al-Akhlaq, his supplication on noble moral traits)
Muwatta Malik, Book 47 (Good Character), hadith 8 (I was sent to perfect good character)
